scenes.title: Previously: MCP client
flow: A server's tool is a Tool

captions.text: Recap of chapter 29: McpClient let your agent use tools it doesn't own.
as_tool turned a server's tool into a normal Tool. Agent didn't change.
The same client reached new and older servers.
And a tool's text is someone else's words, going into your prompt.
Today's black box: a team of agents. The next step, people say. Is it?
Let's open it, and measure it. The number to beat: one agent, 113 of 126.
One new idea. A Tool is just a name, a description and a function.
So the function can run a whole agent, and return its answer as text.
The worker starts with an empty chat. It knows only what the task says.
A manager with two workers, each a whole agent with its own search. Predict: how many model calls?
It worked, and the task passed on word for word. Four model calls, where one agent takes two.
A router is cheaper. One model call picks a worker, and that worker does the whole job.
temperature=0, because this is a decision, not writing.
If the reply is unclear, the first worker gets it.
Four questions: two for the handbook and two for the records. Predict: how many arrive at the right worker?
One of four. Each worker honestly said it didn't know, because it couldn't see the answer. No crash.
So does a team beat one agent? The same eval, three runs of 42 questions, on every setup.
Every real team did worse, and cost more. Splitting created a decision the model can get wrong.
The strict manager reached 102, with more than twice the calls.
The perfect router was told the right worker every time. It only tied, at 113.
One run froze for 13 minutes. We believe this is the same fault, caught later: a reply that repeats itself.
A timeout limits silence, and a runaway is never silent. So OllamaModel now limits length: num_predict.
Research says teams win when work is big and splits cleanly, and warns that wins may just be extra compute.
Hop questions need two facts. Two steps took one agent from 53 to 75, of 150. So extra work is part of it.
A relay reached 93. Its second agent is the same model. The difference is mainly a clean chat.
After one pass they tied at 17, and we wrote that the agent added nothing. Five passes said otherwise.
A second opinion? A fresh reviewer, with its own search, told not to trust the draft. Predict.
It fixed 5 and broke 5. On one model, checking mostly moved the errors around.
Now a pile of independent questions: all in one chat, or one chat each? Predict: which breaks first?
Twenty in one chat got none right. The search results overflowed the window, with no error.
Over 108 questions, one chat each got 93. So here, a split wins.
But a bigger window got 83 in 7 calls, not 221. A team has to beat that too.
Now a job no window can hold: 48 logs, about 60,000 tokens, and this model's limit is 32,768.
Each worker copies matching sentences from one log. Code checks each line, and adds them up.
The team landed on the true total, 175. But every branch was wrong, by 2 to 8.
Every try, on late deliveries. One call read a quarter of the logs, with no error, and copied our example.
Small workers got closest: 3% to 16%. That's the team's real win, and it's still approximate.
A team of 4 big workers was erratic, at 78%. The pieces had to be small.
On run-outs, the small workers were 21% to 28% off. Being 27% off isn't a number for a report.
And plain text search got it exactly right, with no model at all. If code can do it, use code.
Ask in order. Can plain code do it? Then use code. It's exact and free.
Do parts need different permissions? Split for that reason. That's chapter 31.
Does it fit in one call, or a bigger window? One agent. For more thinking, add steps first.
Does it split into small, independent pieces? A team of small workers, and code joins the results.
Five exercises: build the tool, the choice, the count, the split and the chooser. They start failing.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

captions.text: Start with one agent. Split only when you can name what forced you to.
Those counts come from one 7B model on one Mac. Test yours.
